_note: Every address here was independently verified on mainnet (chain 1) via direct RPC calls before being committed — see `observed` on each entry for exactly what was read and when. Nothing here is taken from memory. Pin block 25800000 for all targets (~2026-08-21, safely finalized behind head at verification time) unless noted otherwise.

targets.label: weth9
targets.why: Canonical Wrapped Ether. Immutable since 2015 — no proxy of any kind, no owner, no privileged capability at all. The baseline 'nothing to see here' case.
targets.observed: hasCode=true, bytecodeSize=3124. All EIP-1967/EIP-1822/legacy proxy slots read zero. owner()/pendingOwner() both revert (no Ownable). proxy.pattern=not_a_proxy. powerHolders=[]. unknowns=[], errors=[].

targets.label: aave-pool-addresses-provider
targets.why: Aave v3's PoolAddressesProvider on mainnet. Not upgradeable itself; its own Ownable owner is 0x5300A1a15135EA4dc7aD5a167152C01EFc9b192A, which is itself a contract (Aave governance executor), not an EOA — reduced centralization risk by the day-1 signal we can actually check (full timelock-delay verification is explicitly day-4 scope, not claimed here).
targets.observed: hasCode=true. All EIP-1967/legacy proxy slots read zero (genuinely not upgradeable). owner()=0x5300A1a15135EA4dc7aD5a167152C01EFc9b192A, classified type=contract via getCode. KNOWN LIMITATION surfaced by this fixture: proxy.pattern comes back 'unknown', not 'not_a_proxy', because the contract's own bytecode contains a real DELEGATECALL opcode — not because it's a proxy, but because PoolAddressesProvider deploys child proxies via `new InitializableImmutableAdminUpgradeabilityProxy(...)`, and Solidity embeds that child contract's full initcode (including its real DELEGATECALL) inside the parent's own bytecode. Confirmed by finding a second '6080604052' contract-prologue signature embedded partway through the bytecode. Ripcord's bytecode scan is a linear walk (respecting PUSH-data lengths) with no control-flow reachability analysis, so it cannot distinguish 'opcode this contract would execute' from 'opcode embedded as another contract's creation code.' Documented as a known false-'unknown' in README Limitations rather than suppressed.

targets.label: paid-network-token-proxy-1
targets.why: One of two PAID Network (PAID) token proxies on mainnet, the protocol behind the well-documented March 2021 proxy-admin-key-compromise exploit (~$2.5-3M loss) — a textbook real-world instance of exactly the risk class Ripcord targets: audited code, no bug, an admin key change was enough. Illustrates the asymmetry directly: the token's own business-logic owner is a reasonably-configured 3-of-11 Gnosis Safe, but the separate, more powerful UPGRADE authority (the ProxyAdmin contract) is owned by a single EOA with no timelock — the more dangerous capability is the less protected one.
targets.observed: proxy.pattern=eip1967_transparent, implementation=0x3159810dd4d4d96961f3f04737d53650b6550690, admin=0x8f7e89f9017badba38d541b77e2e4073852d6b8b (an OpenZeppelin ProxyAdmin contract, selectors match ProxyAdmin.sol exactly: getProxyImplementation/upgrade/changeProxyAdmin/owner/transferOwnership). authority.owner=0x5f1bD0Feb0bF7C3ee0cde570f807436D29F4B4b2, classified type=safe, Gnosis Safe v1.1.1, threshold=3, 11 owners. Manually verified beyond day-1 scope (not something Ripcord itself resolves today — dependency-graph traversal through a ProxyAdmin's own owner() is explicitly day-2 scope): calling owner() on the ProxyAdmin (0x8f7e89f9017badba38d541b77e2e4073852d6b8b) itself resolves to 0x3cc21a33fe8ed011a307fd5988f6535bcb3f2ae3, which has no code (a plain EOA) — the true upgrade authority. Ripcord's day-1 output correctly and conservatively stops at classifying the direct admin as type=contract; it does not yet claim to know who controls that contract.

targets.label: paid-network-token-proxy-2
targets.disclosureNote: DAY 2: this is the DEPRECATED v1 token, superseded after the March 2021 exploit. Verified by deployment date via Ripcord's own findDeploymentBlock: this contract deployed at block 11724025 (2021-01-25, i.e. BEFORE the exploit), while paid-network-token-proxy-1 (0x1614...d787) deployed at block 12002538 (2021-03-09, i.e. IN the exploit window) and is therefore the post-incident redeploy. Both report totalSupply 594717455e18 and name/symbol 'PAID Network'/'PAID'. Day-2 guard probing observed that mint(address,uint256) does not revert when called from an unrelated address on this v1 contract (confirmed with realistic non-zero args, so not a zero-args artifact). Per the disclosure policy this was NOT investigated further for exploitability and is NOT published as a vulnerability claim: the report correctly routes it to needsManualVerification and its disclosure.publishable is false, so this fixture is excluded from the published calibration set. The contract is an abandoned pre-migration deployment with no current users, so there is no meaningful disclosure target. The PAID material used in the demo is the power asymmetry from the publicly documented 2021 incident, not this observation.
targets.why: The second PAID Network token proxy on mainnet — same protocol/incident as paid-network-token-proxy-1, but this one's own business-logic owner is directly a plain EOA (no multisig at all), making it the more starkly 'concerning' of the two: a fully single-key-controlled upgradeable token, both for business logic and (per manual follow-up) for upgrades.
targets.observed: proxy.pattern=eip1967_transparent, implementation=0xb828e66eb5b41b9ada9aa42420a6542cd095b9c7, admin=0x7bb7580edb70170daf8a24afc6aaef93db720c24 (ProxyAdmin contract, same selector signature as proxy-1's). authority.owner=0x53bc21D38281D6AcdFE0b92e0B534a19C90344cC, classified type=eoa directly (getCode returns empty). Manually verified beyond day-1 scope: the ProxyAdmin's own owner() resolves to 0x18738290af1aaf96f0acfa945c9c31ab21cd65be, also a plain EOA (no code) — so both the business-logic owner and (one hop past what Ripcord resolves today) the upgrade authority are single EOAs, no multisig, no timelock anywhere in the chain.

targets.label: wasabi-perp-manager
targets.why: Wasabi Protocol's PerpManager proxy on mainnet — the exact protocol and vulnerability class cited in this project's own brief: on 2026-04-30, an attacker took over the 'wasabideployer.eth' EOA, which held sole, unchecked admin authority (no multisig, no timelock) over every upgradeable Wasabi vault, and used it to UUPS-upgrade the perp vaults and LongPool to a malicious implementation, draining ~$4.5-5.9M across four chains in under three minutes. Chosen deliberately as the 'genuinely uncertain' fixture: Ripcord correctly identifies the proxy pattern (real evidence, real slots) but cannot identify the authority (also real, honest, evidence-backed non-detection) — demonstrating 'unknown is never safe' with a real incident rather than a contrived one.
targets.observed: proxy.pattern=eip1967_uups (implementation slot populated, admin slot zero), implementation=0xa8516ff9d132ed3a3c352fe04f05fe117bae97ce. owner() reverts (no Ownable). DEFAULT_ADMIN_ROLE() reverts, and hasRole(keccak256('ADMIN_ROLE'), wasabiDeployerEOA) also reverts — Wasabi does not implement OpenZeppelin's standard AccessControl interface at all; it uses a custom, unrecognised access-control scheme (independently reported as a single ADMIN_ROLE gate on the deployer EOA, but Ripcord's day-1 detectors have no evidence for this — deliberately not asserted in the report). Confirmed 0x5c629f8c0b5368f523c85bfe79d2a8efb64fb0c8 (the reported deployer/attack-vector EOA) has no code, independent of and prior to this fixture's inclusion. authority.owner=null, authority.accessControl.detected=false, powerHolders=[]. Because proxy.isProxy=true but no admin/owner/accessControl was found, build.ts emits an explicit unknowns[] entry (field='authority') stating the proxy IS upgradeable by someone unidentified — the report never lets 'found nothing' silently read as 'nothing to find.'
